implementation_notes: Records give C# the memento type for free: a record's state is its positional member list, `with` performs non-destructive mutation by copying through the record's copy constructor, and value equality makes snapshots directly comparable in tests. The originator holds a record instance, the caretaker a Stack<State> or a bounded queue, and undo is an assignment from the popped value; when history must survive a restart, System.Text.Json serializes the record and deserializes it back. Because a record is shallowly copied, the state must either consist of immutable values or copy its collections in an explicit copy constructor. The classic nested Memento class remains the right shape when nobody outside the originator may construct a state value at all.
pitfalls: Record copies and `with` are shallow: a record holding a List<T> or an array shares it with the original, so later mutations show up inside the snapshot - copy collections in a user-defined copy constructor or use immutable collections.
MemberwiseClone, the classic trick behind ICloneable, is documented as a shallow copy; ICloneable itself says nothing about depth, so callers cannot know whether they received a snapshot or an alias.
JSON round-trips produce new instances and drop what is not serializable (delegates, handles, [JsonIgnore] members), so re-hydration must go through the originator rather than a blind deserialize.
An unbounded Stack grows with every save and keeps whole state graphs alive; bound the history explicitly.

variants.name: Classic nested Memento class (MemberwiseClone era)
variants.idiom_name: private nested Memento class + ICloneable/MemberwiseClone copy
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-records realization: the originator declares a nested Memento class with members only it can see, fills an instance with the state to capture and hands out the result as an opaque handle while keeping the concrete type private. Restoring copies the members back inside the originator, so the caretaker never has to know the state's shape, and MemberwiseClone provides the cheap copy the originator completes by copying the mutable members it owns - the documented pattern is a shallow clone followed by explicit deep copies of the reference members. Choose it when state must not be constructible outside the originator or when the code base predates C# 9.
pitfalls: A nested Memento only hides state while the type stays private: widening a member to expose it (or returning the nested type) turns the wide interface into a public one.
MemberwiseClone shares every reference member; the originator must deep-copy the members it owns and document which ones a snapshot covers.
Handles typed as object cannot be inspected or serialized, so a UI that wants to label history entries needs a small marker interface carrying metadata only.
